Inequalities and Probabilities
Once a pmf (or the required probabilities of the pmf) have been calculated, they are added together
for probabilities that use  >,  ≥,  <,  and  ≤.  For  >  and  <, the probability at the boundary is not added.
The probability of no more than  𝑎:  Pr(𝑋  ≤  𝑎) •
The probability of fewer than  𝑎:  Pr(𝑋  <  𝑎) •
The probability of at least  𝑎  / of no fewer than  𝑎:  Pr(𝑋  ≥  𝑎) •
The probability of more than  𝑎:  Pr(𝑋  >  𝑎) •
Some common phrases involving inequalities include:
Complementary Probabilities with Inequalities
1  =  Pr(𝑋  ≤  𝑎)  +  Pr(𝑋  >  𝑎)
⇒  Pr(𝑋  ≤  𝑎)  =  1  −  Pr(𝑋  >  𝑎)
⇒  Pr(𝑋  >  𝑎)  =  1  −  Pr(𝑋  ≤  𝑎)
1  =  Pr(𝑋  <  𝑎)  +  Pr(𝑋  ≥  𝑎)
⇒  Pr(𝑋  <  𝑎)  =  1  −  Pr(𝑋  ≥  𝑎)
⇒  Pr(𝑋  ≥  𝑎)  =  1  −  Pr(𝑋  <  𝑎)

Two events are independent if the events have no effect on the probability of the other occurring.

Dependent Compound Events

has occured. Sampling without replacement is dependent

Law of Total Probability
The probability of  𝐵  can be determined using
Pr(𝐵)  =  Pr(𝐴  ∩  𝐵)  +  Pr(𝐴ᇱ  ∩  𝐵),  where
Pr(𝐴  ∩  𝐵)  =  Pr(𝐴)  ×  Pr(𝐵|𝐴)  and
Pr(𝐴ᇱ  ∩  𝐵)  =  Pr(𝐴ᇱ)  ×  Pr(𝐵|𝐴ᇱ)
Therefore, the law of total probability is
Pr(𝐵)  =  Pr(𝐴)  ×  Pr(𝐵|𝐴)  +  Pr(𝐴ᇱ)  ×  Pr(𝐵|𝐴ᇱ)

Often we are asked to change use  Pr(𝐵|𝐴)  to determine  Pr(𝐴|𝐵). This can be done by utilising the
multiplication rule and the law of total probability. The best way to do this is using the double ended tree
diagram to determine  Pr(𝐴  ∩  𝐵)  and  Pr(𝐵)  NOT by memorising the formula.

Using the Factor Theorem Attempts to Sketch a Polynomial
For a polynomial with numerous possible rational roots, we can plot the points from the substitutions of
the possible roots into the polynomial to help sketch the graph and narrow down which of the remaining
possible roots are more likely to be a root than the others. This is essentially making a table of values
using  𝑥-values that may be roots rather than picking a generic set of  𝑥  values.
Keep in mind:
Polynomials must be smooth curves, they cannot jump values. Therefore, if one output in negative
and one is positive, then the polynomial must be zero somewhere between.
•
A polynomial of degree  𝑛  will have up to  𝑛  real roots. •
Polynomials with an odd degree and real coefficients must have at least one real root. •
Keep in mind the possible shape(s) of the polynomial you are sketching to reduce the options. If
the shape does not allow for it to turn around again beyond a certain value, do not keep looking
beyond there.
•
It is possible the roots are not rational. If that is the case, you can at least narrow down intervals
for which the  𝑥-intercepts must occur. Bisection method or Newton's method could be used to
approximate the solution of these roots. If two of the roots are not rational, then you can factorise
the polynomial into linear factors for the rational roots and a quadratic factor that can be
factorised with its irrational roots.
•

### Key Features of Graphs

Axis Intercepts
𝑥-intercepts
Points where the graph crosses or touches the  𝑥-
axis.  𝑥-intercepts occur when  𝑦  =  0.
𝑦-intercepts
Points where the graph crosses or touches the  𝑦-
axis.  𝑦-intercepts occur when  𝑥  =  0.
Stationary Points
Points where the gradient of the tangent of the graph at that point is 0.
Maximum Turning Points
Points where the graph changes from increasing to
0 to decreasing. Concave down around this point.
Minimum Turning Points
Points where the graph changes from decreasing
to 0 to increasing. Concave up around this point.
Points of Inflection
Points where the graph changes from concave down to concave up, or vice versa.
Stationary Points of Inflection
Points of inflection and the gradient of the tangent
of the graph at that point is 0.
Non-Stationary Points of Inflection
Points of inflection and the gradient of the tangent
of the graph at that point is not 0.
Asymptotic Behaviour
Vertical Asymptote
As  𝑦  approaches  ∞  and/or  −∞, the  𝑦-value of the
graph approaches the  𝑥-value of the asymptote.
Horizontal Asymptote
As  𝑥  approaches  ∞  and/or  −∞, the  𝑦-value of the
graph approaches the  𝑦-value of the asymptote.
Symmetry of Functions
Even Function
A function that is symmetrical around the  𝑦-axis

Odd Function

Flaws with Newton's Method
Newton's method has flaws: it can stop early, approach the wrong root, or get stuck in a loop.
A terminating sequence will occur if you choose a value of  𝑥,
or reach a value of  𝑥, that is a stationary point. That is,
𝑓ᇱ(𝑥)  =  0  since the denominator cannot be 0.
•
A sequence that approaches the wrong root will occur if  𝑥଴  if
on the wrong side of a nearby stationary point as the tangent
will not point in the direction of desired root.
•
An oscillating sequence will occur if the tangent at  𝑥  =  𝑎
crosses the  𝑥-axis at a point  𝑥  =  𝑏  such that the tangent at
𝑥  =  𝑏  crosses the  𝑥-axis at  𝑥  =  𝑎.
•
Pseudocode for Newton's Method
START
input  function  f(x),  tolerance TOL
input  initial guess x0, max iterations  N
function g(x)  = derivative(f(x),x)
step = 1
while  abs(f(x1)>TOL)  do
if  g(x0) = 0
print  "sequence  terminated at
stationary  point"
STOP
end if
x1 =  x0 -  f(x0)/g(x0)
x0 =  x1
step  = step + 1
if  step  >  N
print  "sequence  did not converge"
STOP
end if
print  "root  = ", x1
STOP

following steps until the function of
the next input outputs a value not

Newton's method running
indefinitely in case it gets stuck in a

Polynomials are the product of linear and power functions with positive integers.

functions being multiplied together. The domain of the product function is set of values that both
functions are defined.

Product of Ordinates  -  Sketching Product Functions
Similar to sum and difference functions, the ordinates of the product function can be found by getting
the product of the ordinates of the two parts. Again, this is very tedious so we generalise.
The product function has an  𝑥-intercept when either graph has an  𝑥-intercept. •
If one function's ordinate is 1, the product function's ordinate equals the other function's at that
point.
•
If one function's ordinate is  −1, the product function's ordinate equals the opposite the other
function's at that point.
•
If the two graph are both positive or both negative, the product function will be positive. •
If the two graphs have different signs, the product function will be negative. •

Pseudocode and Algorithms:
### Pseudocode and Algorithms

Pseudocode and Algorithms
We can program computers to perform certain algorithms. However, there are several languages
that can be used for differing purposes to tell a computer what to do. So, if we don't want to write in
a specific language (that has particular conventions that others may not match), we write the code in
a more plain language form called pseudocode.
The particular details of the formatting of code is called syntax.
If the formatting is incorrect, the code cannot be correctly read (parsed).
Sequencing
An algorithm is performed line by line from the pseudocode.
Each successive line will be performed in turn.
We start and end our pseudocode with  START  … STOP
To set a variable to a specific value, we write  variable  ←  value to  set  at
To set a variable that we can input a value into, we write  INPUT  variable
To perform an operation, we can use the operation symbols  +, -,  *,  /.
Other functions can be written in words such as  squareroot().
To have the algorithm write out a particular result or statement, we write
print "show this text"  // prints  exactly what  is in  the  ""
print variable  // prints  the  variable's  value
print "variable =  ", variable  // prints  variable  = its  value
Example
The following pseudocode can multiply two numbers that are input by the user.
START
input  number1,  number2
product = number1*number2
print  product
STOP

Repetition
There are two ways we can repeat steps of an algorithm:
repeat the steps a predetermined amount of times, in which case we use a 'for' loop •
repeat the steps until a condition is met, in which case we use a 'while' loop. •
The syntax for a 'for' loop is written below.
FOR  condition
do this
change value for condition
END FOR
The syntax for a 'while' loop is written below.
WHILE  condition  DO
do this until  condition  no
longer true
END WHILE

ten terms of the sequence "double, subtract

i = i + 1
print  x0
end for
STOP

### Sum and Difference Functions

Sum and Difference Functions
Functions that are comprised of basic functions added or subtracted from each other.
Polynomials are the sum and difference of power functions with positive integer powers.
Sum Function
The ordinates, or  𝑦-values, of a sum function are defined as the sum of the ordinates of the functions
being added together.
The domain of the sum function is set of values that both functions are defined.
(𝑓  +  𝑔)(𝑥)  =  𝑓(𝑥)  +  𝑔(𝑥),  𝑑௙ା௚  =  𝑑௙  ∩  𝑑௚
Difference Function
Difference functions can be written as a sum function with the reflection of the function in the  𝑥-axis.
(𝑓  −  𝑔)(𝑥)  =  𝑓(𝑥)  −  𝑔(𝑥)  =  𝑓(𝑥)  +  ൫−𝑔(𝑥)൯,  𝑑௙ି  ௚  =  𝑑௙  ∩  𝑑௚

Addition of Ordinates  -  Sketching Sum and Difference Functions
To sketch the graph of a sum or difference function, in particular where the two functions are not
from the same family and cannot be combined to something simpler, we add the ordinates (𝑦-values)
of each coordinate from both graphs together. However, this becomes painfully slow. We can make
some generalisations based on the graphs of the two parts to make the sketching simpler.
If one of the graphs is positive (above the  𝑥-axis) and the other is negative (below the  𝑥-axis),
then the sum function must lie between the two graphs. In particular, the sum function will
have an  𝑥-intercept when the two functions have the same value with different signs.
•
If one graph has an  𝑥-intercept, then the sum function's ordinate will equal the other function's
at that point. The sum function will also approach the other graph the same direction the
function approaches the  𝑥-axis.
•
If either graph has a  vertical  asymptote, the sum function also has that asymptote. •

### Systems of Simultaneous Linear Equations

Systems of Simultaneous Linear Equations
A set of linear equations that must be solved together to find the values of all unknowns. To solve
for all unknowns, the number of unknowns must be the same as the number of unique equations.
For example, when there are two linear equations that share two variables, they can be solved
together to find the values of both variables that satisfy both equations simultaneously.
Graphical Method for Two Linear Equations with Two Variables
Graphically, the solution to a pair of
simultaneous linear equations is the
coordinate where the graphs of both
lines intersect. So, we can solve the
equations simultaneously by
sketching the lines of both equations
and read off the coordinate of the
intersection point.
Example
𝑦  =  2𝑥  −  3
𝑦  =  −5𝑥  +  4
The graphs intersect at  (1,  −1).
∴  𝑥  =  1,  𝑦  =  −1

Since the two equations share the same value for their unknowns, we can use substitution
between the equations involving the variables. This may include:
equating a variable from both equations, that is,
make  𝑦  =  𝑦  if the equations are both  𝑦  =  an expression, or ○
make  𝑥  =  𝑥  if the equations are both  𝑥  =  expression ○

substitute one equation into the other when one equation is  𝑦  =  or  𝑥  = •
The idea is to reduce the equations to one unknown, find its value, then use it to find the value of
the other unknown by substituting it into one of the original equations.

### Transformations of the Plane and Functions

Transformations of the Plane
In Geometry, we can transform shapes (and the plane) by using transformations. Three of which are:
dilations (enlarging or shrinking a shape), reflections (mirroring across a line), and translations
(sliding). In Coordinate Geometry, the same transformations can be applied to points and graphs.
Dilations involve multiplying the  𝑥  or  𝑦  values by a scale
factor. That is, you stretch it until it is a number of time
larger (e.g. twice as large), or you squash it until it is a
fraction of the size (e.g. half as large).
There are two ways of phrasing dilations:
dilation by a factor of  𝑎  in the  𝑥/𝑦  direction, or •
dilation by a factor of  𝑎  away from the  𝑦/𝑥-axis. •
Reflections involve multiplying the  𝑥  or  𝑦  values by a
negative. That is because multiplying (or dividing) by a
negative number reflects a number from the positive
side of a number line to the negative and vice versa.
Translations involve adding a number to the  𝑥  or  𝑦
values. That is, you uniformally move every point the
same amount in the same direction.

The Sum of Solutions of Trigonometric Equations
For most angles, the sequential solutions of sine and cosine equations alternate adding and subtracting the
base angle from a multiple of  𝜋. So, the sum of the solutions will be the sum of the multiples of  𝜋  for sine and
